items.title: The Long Flight of the Monarchs
items.text:
Every fall, something strange happens in the fields and
backyards of eastern North America. Monarch butterflies
that have spent the summer drifting from flower to
flower suddenly change. They turn south, and they keep
flying for weeks.

A monarch weighs less than a gram. Yet some of these
insects travel as far as 3,000 miles to reach their
winter home. They can cover 50 to 100 miles in a single
day, and the whole trip may take up to two months.
Monarchs from the eastern part of the continent gather
in the mountains of central Mexico. There they settle on
the branches of oyamel fir trees, high up where the air
stays cool. Tens of thousands of butterflies can cluster
on a single tree, so thickly that the branches look as
if they have grown orange leaves. Monarchs from the West
spend the winter on the California coast instead,
resting in groves of pine, cypress, and eucalyptus
trees.

The butterflies that make this journey are not ordinary
monarchs. A monarch born in early summer lives only two
to five weeks. The last generation of the year is
different. It can live as long as nine months, long
enough to fly south, wait out the winter, and start
north again in spring. Scientists think these
butterflies use the position of the sun and the changing
weather to know when it is time to leave.

No single butterfly makes the whole round trip. When
warm days return, the monarchs leave Mexico and fly
north, laying eggs on milkweed plants along the way. The
caterpillars that hatch feed on milkweed leaves, grow
into butterflies, fly a little farther north, and lay
eggs of their own. It takes three or four generations to
reach the northern United States and Canada. By late
summer the fields of the North are full of monarchs
again, and a new generation is getting ready to fly
3,000 miles to trees it has never seen.
items.source: Facts verified against the U.S. Forest Service pages 'Monarch Butterfly Migration and Overwintering' (fs.usda.gov/wildflowers/pollinators/Monarch_Butterfly/migration/index.shtml) and 'Monarch Butterfly Biology' (fs.usda.gov/wildflowers/pollinators/Monarch_Butterfly/biology/index.shtml), and the National Park Service article 'Monarch Butterfly' (nps.gov/articles/monarch-butterfly.htm). Original prose authored for Sheila ISEE.

items.title: The Fossil Hunter of Lyme Regis
items.text:
Mary Anning was born in 1799 in Lyme Regis, a town on
the south coast of England. The cliffs beside the town
are packed with fossils of sea creatures from the time
of the dinosaurs. Today that shore is known as the
Jurassic Coast.

Mary's father, Richard, was a cabinetmaker who collected
fossils. He taught Mary how to spot them on the beach
and how to clean them, and he sold them from his shop.
Fossil collecting was a fashionable hobby then, and
people paid for curiosities to display at home. Richard
died in 1810, leaving his family poor and in debt.
Mary's mother encouraged her to keep selling what she
found.

In the autumn of 1811, when Mary was twelve, her brother
Joseph found a strange fossil skull. About a year later
Mary found the rest of the animal and carefully dug out
its skeleton, five meters long. It was an ichthyosaur, a
sea reptile whose name means "fish lizard." In 1823 she
found the first complete skeleton of a plesiosaur,
another sea reptile. A French scientist who studied a
drawing of it doubted that it was real. Once he realized
it was genuine, Mary and her family were treated as true
experts. In 1828 she uncovered a jumble of bones that
turned out to be a pterosaur, a flying reptile. It was
the first ever found outside Germany.

Mary had little schooling, but she could read, and she
taught herself geology and anatomy. One visitor wrote in
her diary in 1824 that the moment Mary found a bone, she
knew what animal it came from. Yet the scientists who
bought her fossils and wrote about them often left her
name out. The Geological Society of London did not allow
women to join until 1908. Mary died in 1847, at the age
of forty-seven. In 2022, after a campaign led by an
eleven-year-old girl, a statue of Mary and her dog was
unveiled in Lyme Regis.
items.source: Facts verified against the Natural History Museum, London, 'Mary Anning: the unsung hero of fossil discovery' (nhm.ac.uk/discover/mary-anning-unsung-hero.html) and the University of California Museum of Paleontology, 'Mary Anning (1799-1847)' (ucmp.berkeley.edu/history/anning.html). Original prose authored for Sheila ISEE.

items.title: The Sound of Snow
items.text:
When you watch a movie, the crunch of footsteps on
gravel or the creak of a door seems to come from the
picture itself. Most of the time, however, it does not.
"Nearly every small sound you hear in a film was made
later, by a person in a room like this one," the sound
artist Ms. Castellano told the fifth graders visiting
her studio last spring.

The studio looked like an extremely messy garage. There
were trays of gravel and sand on the floor, a rack of
shoes in every size, a bathtub, and shelves crowded with
objects that seemed to have nothing in common: coconut
shells, a leather glove, a bag of cornstarch, celery, a
broken umbrella.

Ms. Castellano played a short film clip with the sound
turned off. A woman walked down a snowy lane, stopped,
and snapped a branch from a tree. Then the clip played
again, and this time Ms. Castellano made every sound
herself while she watched the screen. For the footsteps
in snow she squeezed a bag of cornstarch in her fists,
and the crunch was so real that several students glanced
down at their own feet. For the branch she snapped a
stalk of celery beside the microphone. "Your ears
believe whatever your eyes tell them," she said.

Then the students took their turns at the microphone.
One boy galloped two coconut shells across a tray of
dirt to make a horse, and another flapped the leather
glove to make a bird taking off. The hardest sound
turned out to be the simplest one. No one could produce
a convincing footstep until Ms. Castellano pointed out
that real people do not walk like a ticking clock. They
slow down, hesitate, and shift their weight. When Mina
finally got it right, stepping in place on a plank with
her eyes fixed on the screen, the whole room went quiet.
For a moment it sounded exactly as if someone were
crossing a wooden porch at night.

items.title: The Bus With No Engine
items.text:
At a quarter to eight on Wednesday mornings, a bus pulls
up at the corner of Maple and Third. It has no engine,
no doors, and no driver. It is a bike bus: a long
procession of children on bicycles, riding to school
together behind a parent who leads the way.

The idea is simple. A grown-up leader rides at the
front, following the same route every week and stopping
at the same corners, just as a real bus does. Children
wait at the "stops" with their bikes and helmets and
join the line as it passes. Another adult rides at the
very back and is called the caboose. In between, the
line can stretch for a whole block. A speaker strapped
to the leader's bike plays music, so the group can be
heard coming before it can be seen.

This bike bus started small. On the first morning only
four riders showed up, and one of them was the leader's
own son. He made the ride anyway, music playing, waving
at people on their porches. By the end of the fall there
were nineteen riders, and in the spring the line grew to
more than thirty. Drivers along the route learned to
anticipate it. Some now wait at the corners with their
windows down to listen.

Riding in a group changes what a child is allowed to do.
A nine-year-old who would never be permitted to bike
alone across a busy street can cross it with twenty
others and two adults. The rules are strict: helmets on,
a hand signal before every turn, and no passing the
leader. A rider who misses a stop can usually catch up
at the next one, because the bus rolls slowly enough for
the youngest legs.

On rainy days the bus still runs. The riders arrive at
school with wet socks and red cheeks, and the bike rack,
which once held three or four bikes, is full before the
first bell.

items.title: The Sixth Hen
items.text:
Mrs. Dombrowski was away for three days, and Wren had
the responsibility of looking after her six hens. The
instructions were on an index card taped inside the coop
door: fill the water, scatter the feed, collect the
eggs, and shut the door at dusk. "The door is the
important part," Mrs. Dombrowski had explained.
"Whatever comes into a yard at night is not coming for
the eggs."

On the first evening, five hens filed up the ramp
without any encouragement as the daylight faded, and
settled on the perch inside. The sixth, a speckled brown
hen called Pepper, remained in the middle of the yard.
She regarded Wren as if Wren were the one who was late.

Wren approached cautiously with her arms outstretched.
Pepper trotted left, so Wren followed. Pepper went
right, then under the lilac bush, then behind the rain
barrel, where she scratched at the dirt as though
nothing unusual had happened. By the time Wren had
chased her twice around the yard, her hair was tangled
with lilac leaves and the sky had faded from pink to
gray. She collapsed on the back step to recover her
breath. Pepper walked calmly up the ramp and disappeared
inside.

On the second evening Wren rattled a handful of corn in
a tin cup, and five hens came hurrying. Pepper observed
from the fence post until the corn was gone, then
returned to her scratching. Wren waited patiently
without moving. When the first star appeared, Pepper
went in.

On the third evening Wren brought a book and settled on
the step before the sun had even reached the rooftops.
The hens pecked around her shoes while she read one
chapter, then another, and she never once glanced at the
speckled hen. The yard turned blue, then gray, and there
was a gentle thump on the ramp. Wren counted six shadowy
shapes on the perch and slid the latch home. Above the
coop, the first star was out, exactly where it had been
the night before.
